observations.observed: A large well-defined thin-walled cavitary lesion is present in the right mid-lung zone, approximately 8-10 cm in diameter. An air-fluid level occupies the lower third of the cavity. Irregular crumpled soft-tissue material is visible floating superiorly within the cavity, consistent with a collapsed endocyst membrane — the water-lily sign. All three components (round cyst, air-fluid level, floating membrane) are present and assessable.

observations.observed: The image is a PA chest radiograph showing bilateral lung fields, mediastinum, shoulder girdles, and upper abdomen. No pelvis or groin structures are visible. Skeletal maturity is appropriate for an adult aged 19-39: no visible growth plates, bones appear mature. Symmetric clavicles, scapulae, and ribs are present without duplication or garbling. One cardiac shadow is present. One hemidiaphragm per side is visible. Rib pairs appear symmetric and correctly numbered without forking or floating ribs. Lung markings branch and taper appropriately. No lettering or markers are present on the film.

findings: Large well-defined thin-walled cavitary lesion in the right mid-lung zone, approximately 8-10 cm in diameter, with an air-fluid level occupying roughly the lower third of the cavity and irregular soft-tissue material visible superiorly within the cavity (possible intracavitary mass or debris)
The right lung otherwise shows increased interstitial markings around the cavity
Left lung field appears clear with normal vascular markings
Mediastinum appears midline; trachea is central
Cardiac silhouette is not clearly demarcated on the left due to apparent left lower lobe opacity or elevated left hemidiaphragm; a gastric bubble is visible beneath the left hemidiaphragm
Costophrenic angles: right appears blunted, left is partially obscured
Bony thorax: ribs, clavicles, and visible shoulder girdle structures appear intact without obvious lytic or blastic lesions
No visible pleural effusion on the right above the diaphragm; right hemidiaphragm is partially obscured by the cavity
differential: Pulmonary hydatid cyst (Echinococcus) with water-lily sign — the irregular floating membrane within the air-fluid-containing cavity is highly characteristic
Lung abscess — thick or thin walled cavity with air-fluid level, possible in pyogenic infection
Post-primary tuberculosis with cavitation — upper/mid lobe cavitary disease with air-fluid level, though the very large size and thin wall favor hydatid
anatomyConcerns: The left cardiac border is poorly defined, which may represent left lower lobe collapse/consolidation or could reflect patient rotation or suboptimal inspiration, though overall projection appears reasonably standard PA

The very large size of the cavitary lesion (occupying a substantial portion of the right hemithorax) compresses surrounding lung but does not appear to shift the mediastinum, which is anatomically plausible for a slow-growing cyst
Air-fluid level within a cavity of this size raises concern for rupture of a previously intact cyst; the floating membrane-like material is a real finding, not an artifact

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The large thin-walled cavitary lesion in the right mid-lung with an air-fluid level and the characteristic crumpled floating membrane visible superiorly within the cavity (water-lily sign) is the discriminating feature that strongly favors pulmonary hydatid cyst over lung abscess or TB cavity. The floating membrane is the key distinguishing finding not typical of abscess or TB. The left lower lobe opacity/elevated left hemidiaphragm is explainable by mass effect from the large cyst displacing structures. The cardiac border silhouette loss on the left is consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis secondary to compression. No unexplained additional lesions are present.
